title: JPM, BofA Eye Payments Deal — Why JPMorgan, Bank Of America And Other Banks Want Fiserv’s Debit Network - Stocktwits
content: Fiserv (FISV) share price gained 4% after-hours amid a report that several top financial institutions are looking to acquire a network owned by the firm to bypass federal caps on debit card transaction fees. Wall Street giants, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and PNC Financial Services Group, have engaged in early, tentative discussions to buy a proprietary debit-card processing network from financial technology company Fiserv, according to an exclusive report by The Wall Street Journal. The move comes as banks look to replicate an edge gained by Capital One Financial following its massive $50.6-billion acquisition of Discover Financial, which granted the lender its own direct-to-merchant payment rails. At the center of the industry’s interest is a specific section of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act known as the Durbin Amendment. The federal rule caps the interchange fees that institutions with $10 billion or more in assets can charge merchants when a consumer swipes a debit card. But under the current legal framework, if a bank owns the underlying network infrastructure, it is legally exempt from government-imposed fee limits. Consumer banks in the U.S. have fiercely fought the Durbin amendment, stating that they lose billions in revenue and are forced to eliminate popular customer perks, such as debit-card reward programs. Merchants and consumer advocacy groups have countered the claims, maintaining that lower interchange fees have directly translated to lower retail prices for the public, as per WSJ. Fiserv shares have plummeted around 70% from its 2025 highs. This decline is attributed to several factors, including a sharp deceleration in organic growth, intensifying competition in the payment point-of-sale (PoS) sector, and executive-level instability following several CEO changes. Furthermore, the company is facing significant pressure from activist investors calling for asset divestiture. However, Fiserv, is an important fintech middleman that owns two major transaction processing networks, STAR and Accel. Shares of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals (CRNX) surged nearly 100% in after-hours trading on Monday after Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX) announced it will buy the company for about $10 billion. The deal values Crinetics at $85 per share in cash, representing a potential upside of about 100% from the stock’s closing price on Monday. Vertex said the acquisition will strengthen its pipeline and could eventually add around $5 billion in annual revenue. The deal is expected to close later this year, in the third quarter, subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions. VRTX stock was down 2% after-hours at the time of writing. Crinetics focuses on developing treatments for endocrine diseases — conditions related to hormones and glands. Its main product, PALSONIFY (paltusotine), treats acromegaly, a rare disorder that causes excessive growth. The company has additional drugs in its pipeline targeting other hormone-related conditions, such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Vertex, best known for its successful cystic fibrosis medicines, has been looking to expand beyond that area. The company said the move supports its goal of delivering innovative treatments across multiple diseases and added that it expects the deal to be accretive to adjusted operating income in 2029. Vertex will finance the deal using a combination of cash on hand and debt. The deal is one of the largest this year in the biotech sector, in the league of Sun Pharma's acquisition of Organon and AbbVie's acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics. Hertz Global Holdings (HTZ) share price dropped 3.3% on Monday to a record low, marking the ninth straight session of declines. The drop has intensified short-selling pressure on the stock, data from S3 Partners showed. The dramatic drop was set off by a multi-pronged financial update that severely disappointed Wall Street. Hertz issued a profit warning and reported preliminary second-quarter adjusted corporate EBITDA that missed consensus analyst expectations. Following the announcements, the stock plunged a record 41% in a single session—marking its steepest one-day decline since its 2021 post-bankruptcy relisting—before continuing its downward trajectory. As the stock rapidly devalued, bearish traders moved in quickly to maximize their positions. As of Thursday's close, more than 56% of Hertz’s float has been borrowed by traders betting on its stock price falling further, S3 Partners data showed as reported by Bloomberg. “Short interest has increased dramatically,” said Ihor Dusaniwsky, managing director at S3 told Bloomberg. Hertz has seen an additional 13.7 million shares shorted — worth $30 million — since June 24, according to Dusaniwsky. That means about 20% of short positions have been opened in less than two weeks. Hertz stock fell to record lows as concerns about the company’s rising vehicle depreciation costs and weakness in the used-car market have triggered a sell-off. The rental car company also slashed its second-quarter earnings forecast to a range of $50 million to $80 million, citing unexpected weakness in the used car market. Last month, the company also completed a $350 million secured exchangeable notes offering, with an option to raise an additional $50 million, which it said would help boost liquidity and financial flexibility as it advances its turnaround efforts. JP Morgan said the combination of Prudential's growth outlook and valuation supported its positive stance on the shares. The bank's assessment also highlighted the potential for stronger capital returns, with free cash generation providing scope for its forecasts to move higher. title: JP Morgan Weighs In on Indonesia's 2027 State Budget Draft - en.tempo.co
content: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - J.P. Morgan Indonesia stated that the 2027 State Budget (APBN) reflects a constructive balance. The financial services firm, part of U.S.-based JPMorgan Chase, believes this balance strikes a middle ground between sustaining economic growth and maintaining fiscal discipline. "Amid ongoing global uncertainty, Indonesia's economic resilience, strong domestic liquidity, and various ongoing reform efforts remain the foundation for long-term growth potential," JP Morgan Indonesia CEO Gioshia Ralie said in a written statement quoted on Friday, September 4, 2026. Under the macroeconomic assumptions for the 2027 draft state budget, the government targets economic growth of 6.0 percent and inflation at 2.5 percent. Meanwhile, the exchange rate is projected at Rp17,500 per U.S. dollar, with 10-year government bond yields expected around 6.9 percent. State revenue in the 2027 draft budget is targeted at Rp3,426.0 trillion, marking a 6.8 percent increase from the previous year. This figure comprises tax revenue of Rp2,908.0 trillion, non-tax state revenue of Rp517.4 trillion, and grants totaling Rp700 billion. State expenditure under the 2027 draft budget is planned at Rp4,097.2 trillion, up 3.9 percent from the previous year. This allocation includes central government spending of Rp3,362.2 trillion and regional transfers of Rp735.0 trillion. On the financing side, the 2027 budget deficit is targeted at Rp671.2 trillion, or 2.40 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). This figure marks a reduction from this year's target of Rp689.1 trillion, or 2.68 percent of GDP. According to Gioshia, the lower fiscal deficit target signals a cautious fiscal stance. However, over the medium term, the declining ratio of state revenue to GDP and an escalating interest payment burden remain key challenges for Indonesia's fiscal outlook. "In general, a more conservative fiscal stance can help dampen volatility in Indonesia's stock market and exchange rate," he said. On the other hand, Gioshia noted that substantial non-interest and subsidy spending indicates sustained support for key programs. However, the government may be forced to scale back subsidies if global energy prices surge. Gioshia stressed that sustained growth in Indonesia will depend on the efficiency of public spending and larger private sector investments. "It depends on the effectiveness of government spending and the ability to attract larger private investments through foreign direct investment (FDI), deregulation, and non-budget complementary funding," he said. In the medium term, Gioshia noted that private sector investment will serve as the primary growth driver. Furthermore, fiscal resources have been channeled into priority sectors. Enhanced spending efficiency, foreign direct investment, and regulatory reforms are seen as vital avenues for attracting private capital. "Investments from SOEs and Danantara can complement central government spending, helping broaden the capital base needed to support higher growth," he said. Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa previously noted that the global economy in 2027 is expected to face continued high uncertainty. While global economic growth is projected to improve, it will still encounter structural and cyclical risks that weigh on overall performance. "The world economy in 2027 is expected to navigate complex dynamics with high levels of uncertainty," he said during a working meeting with the House of Representatives Budget Committee in Jakarta on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Nevertheless, the former Chairperson of the Indonesia Deposit Insurance Corporation (LPS) Board of Commissioners emphasized that Indonesia's economy remains resilient and demonstrates solid fundamentals. In the first half of 2026, Purbaya added, the economy expanded by 5.45 percent year-on-year. This growth was driven by household consumption, rising investment, and supportive government policy. According to Purbaya, fiscal policy and the state budget are vital tools for safeguarding stability. "Fiscal policy and the state budget strategy are crucial to maintaining macroeconomic stability and realizing prosperity for all Indonesians," he said. Purbaya noted that the 2027 draft budget aims to foster higher growth through economic and fiscal strategies centered on eight national priority clusters. These eight programs include food security; energy and water self-sufficiency; education; healthcare; downstreaming and industrialization; infrastructure, housing, and disaster resilience; rural and grassroots economies; and poverty reduction. In 2027, Purbaya assured, the government will maintain the health, credibility, and sustainability of the state budget. "[This will be achieved] through enhanced state revenue, higher quality and more efficient spending, as well as innovative, prudent budget financing," he said. Traders across Wall Street spent the session parsing the Labor Department's August employment report, a release that has taken on outsized importance after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivered a notably hawkish message at the Jackson Hole gathering. Economists had penciled in a modest gain in nonfarm payrolls alongside a steady unemployment rate, and the dynamic this cycle has effectively inverted the usual reaction pattern: a firmer print now reads as the hawkish outcome that keeps a rate increase on the table, while a softer number would ease pressure on rate-setters. For money-center banking groups such as JPMorgan Chase, the rate trajectory carries direct implications for net interest earnings, deposit costs and the pace of lending across consumer and commercial franchises. Desks across the banking group's trading floor have been positioning around the prospect of a September move, with commentary pointing to elevated volatility in rate-sensitive corners of the market through the gathering. Beyond the Southwest tie-up, the banking group's card and payments arm continues to widen its footprint across travel, dining and everyday spending categories. The Sapphire-branded lounge network has already expanded into several major airports, and the Southwest partnership represents an extension of that playbook into a low-cost carrier segment the bank had not previously served directly. Card spending across premium and mass-market portfolios has remained resilient through the summer months, with travel and entertainment categories showing particular strength even as broader consumer spending growth has moderated. Executives have pointed to the durability of the American consumer as a supportive backdrop for the card business heading into the back half of the calendar year. Chief Executive Jamie Dimon has repeatedly framed artificial intelligence as a transformational force set to touch virtually every function at the banking group, from fraud detection to software engineering to customer service. Dimon has said the technology deployment has already paid for itself through meaningful cost savings, describing the early gains as merely the tip of the iceberg for a much larger transformation still ahead. Operations teams are reportedly handling a noticeably higher volume of accounts per employee, fraud-related costs per unit have declined, and software engineering productivity has climbed as generative tools are woven into daily workflows. The banking group has signaled that technology spending, including artificial intelligence, data infrastructure and cloud computing, will remain a priority even as expense discipline stays a talking point on earnings calls. Dealmaking activity across Wall Street has shown renewed vigor this year, with mergers and acquisitions advisory work, equity issuance and debt underwriting all contributing to a broadly constructive environment for capital-markets and advisory operations. JPMorgan Chase's own advisory and underwriting franchise has benefited from this backdrop, alongside continued strength in equities and fixed-rate trading desks. Corporate clients have continued to bring complex, strategically important transactions to the banking group's advisory teams, a trend executives have cited as evidence of durable client relationships even amid periodic bouts of geopolitical uncertainty. Trading revenue across both equities and rate-and-credit products has stayed a meaningful contributor to quarterly results. The consumer and community banking segment remains the largest single contributor to firmwide results, spanning branch banking, home lending, auto finance and small-business banking. Deposit balances have stabilized after a period of migration toward higher-yielding alternatives, and executives have noted that checking and savings relationships continue to grow across both digital and branch channels. Delinquency trends across card and auto portfolios have stayed within ranges the banking group has described as manageable, even as household budgets face pressure from elevated costs of living. Digital engagement metrics, including mobile app usage and digital account opening, continue to climb as more everyday banking activity shifts away from physical branches. JPMorgan Chase has maintained a capital cushion that executives describe as comfortably above regulatory minimums, giving the banking group flexibility to keep funding both organic growth initiatives and capital returned to stockholders through dividends and buybacks. The banking group has a long history of steadily raising its quarterly dividend, a pattern management has signaled intent to continue barring an unexpected shock to the broader economy. Buyback activity has continued at a measured pace, with management framing share repurchases as one tool among several for deploying excess capital, alongside continued spending on technology, branch expansion and the newly announced travel ecosystem tie-up with Southwest. Market participants tracking US Financial Stocks have highlighted a broader rotation toward banking groups with diversified revenue streams spanning consumer, commercial and capital-markets operations, a structure that has historically cushioned against downturns concentrated in any single business line. JPMorgan Chase's scale across nearly every major financial services category has repeatedly been cited as a structural advantage relative to smaller, more narrowly focused peers. Digital-first competitors and fintech entrants continue to chip away at specific niches such as payments and small-business lending, prompting established banking groups to accelerate their own digital roadmaps rather than cede ground. The competitive response has included expanded mobile capabilities, faster account opening and continued experimentation with artificial intelligence-driven customer service tools. Technology spending at JPMorgan Chase spans cloud migration, cybersecurity hardening and a growing suite of internally built artificial intelligence tools deployed across trading, research and back-office functions. Executives have described the spending envelope as among the largest in the banking group's peer set, framing it as a durable structural advantage rather than a discretionary expense that shrinks during leaner periods. Cybersecurity has remained a persistent area of emphasis given the scale of the banking group's digital footprint and the sensitivity of the data it manages on behalf of millions of consumer and institutional clients. Executives have described fraud prevention as an area where artificial intelligence tools have already produced measurable efficiency gains. JPMorgan Chase continues to be viewed among money-center peers as the largest domestic banking group by assets, a position that affords scale advantages in technology spending, deposit gathering and capital-markets execution. Rival banking groups have pursued their own combinations of dividend growth, buyback programs and digital spending to stay competitive, but JPMorgan Chase's breadth across consumer, commercial and capital-markets businesses remains a frequently cited differentiator. The competitive dynamic has intensified as regional and community banking groups pursue niche strategies while the largest national franchises lean into scale, brand recognition and technology spending to defend market share across deposits, cards and lending. The rate trajectory set by the Federal Reserve remains among the most closely watched variables for the banking sector broadly, given its direct bearing on net interest earnings, loan demand and deposit pricing. Chair Warsh's hawkish tone at Jackson Hole has fueled speculation that officials may move sooner rather than later, though a softer August employment reading could still push a decision toward the following gathering. Regulatory discussions around capital requirements for the largest banking groups continue in the background, with executives across the industry periodically weighing in on proposed changes. JPMorgan Chase has generally argued that excessive capital requirements could constrain lending capacity at a time when credit availability matters for broader economic activity. JPMorgan Chase traces its modern form to a long series of combinations among some of the oldest banking names in the country, a lineage executives regularly invoke when discussing the scale and durability of the current franchise. That history has shaped a culture that management describes as fortress-like, built around maintaining ample capital and liquidity buffers well beyond what regulators require. The banking group has weathered multiple economic cycles, including periods of sharp market stress, and has typically emerged from those episodes with an enlarged market share as smaller or weaker competitors struggled to keep pace with technology spending and capital demands. Across its commercial and corporate banking franchise, JPMorgan Chase has continued to emphasize deep, multi-decade client relationships that span lending, treasury services and capital-markets access. Executives have described this integrated model, sometimes referred to internally as the universal banking approach, as a key reason clients consolidate an increasing share of their financial activity with the banking group. Middle-market and small-business clients have also been a focus area, with the banking group expanding dedicated banking teams and digital tools aimed at simplifying cash management, lending and payments for smaller enterprises that historically relied on regional lenders. Beyond the employment data, broader macroeconomic indicators including inflation readings, consumer spending trends and business capital spending are all feeding into the debate over the Federal Reserve stance. Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks emphasized inflation-related concerns far more heavily than labor-market commentary, according to a tally circulated among Wall Street economics teams, reinforcing the view that price pressures remain the dominant consideration for policymakers. Energy prices, housing costs and wage growth all remain variables market participants are tracking as they attempt to gauge how much room the Federal Reserve has to maneuver at its upcoming gathering, with implications that extend well beyond the banking sector into broader equity and bond markets. Heading into the closing months of the year, JPMorgan Chase appears focused on balancing continued spending on travel and payments partnerships, artificial intelligence deployment and disciplined capital management against a still-uncertain rate backdrop. The Southwest lounge tie-up adds another dimension to a card and payments franchise that already ranks among the largest in the country. With the S&P 500 index near record territory and money-center banking groups broadly participating in this year's advance, JPMorgan Chase's combination of scale, technology spending and diversified revenue streams continues to draw attention from market participants assessing how the sector navigates the next phase of the rate cycle. Regional and community banking groups have increasingly leaned on niche strategies, including localized service models and targeted small-business lending, as they compete against the scale advantages enjoyed by JPMorgan Chase and other national franchises. Executives at smaller institutions have periodically pointed to the technology spending gap as one of the more difficult competitive challenges to close. JPMorgan Chase has continued to expand its branch footprint into markets where it previously had a limited physical presence, part of a broader strategy to combine national scale with a growing local presence, a combination executives describe as difficult for smaller competitors to replicate given the capital required. Surveys of banking clients have repeatedly ranked JPMorgan Chase among the most trusted names in American banking, a reputation executives describe as an asset that pays dividends across every business line, from attracting deposits to winning advisory mandates. The banking group has invested heavily in brand marketing tied to its Chase retail franchise, reinforcing that trust among everyday consumers. Institutional and corporate clients have echoed similar sentiment, with executives noting that brand strength and balance-sheet scale often factor into decisions about which banking group to select for the most complex, multi-year financing relationships. JPMorgan Chase employs a workforce numbering in the hundreds of thousands across retail branches, technology centers, trading floors and corporate offices spanning the country and beyond, a scale executives describe as both an operational strength and a continual management challenge. Training programs aimed at reskilling employees for artificial intelligence-augmented roles have expanded, part of a broader effort to prepare the workforce for a banking group increasingly reliant on automated tools. The banking group has also continued to expand its presence in newer markets domestically, opening branch locations in regions where it historically had limited retail presence, part of a strategy executives describe as extending the national brand into underserved geographies while deepening deposit gathering capacity nationwide. Energy markets and term premiums are connected in a way they haven’t been before. Executive Director, Global Investment Strategist, J.P. Morgan Private Bank The upward march in bond yields continues to drive the market narrative, but the logic has shifted. The move began in the early summer with a Federal Reserve (Fed) that investors initially perceived as hawkish, but a series of softer jobs and inflation reports has cast it in a different light. Now, the drivers look a little different: They’re a combination of worries around global fiscal deficits, an increase in hyperscaler issuance and a rise in refined product prices. And that’s on top of U.S. economic growth. Using a sign-restriction model that determines the drivers of Treasury yields on any given day based on how yields behave relative to inflation expectations, the dollar and equity markets, different combinations can help distinguish whether higher yields reflect stronger growth, rising term premiums or changing expectations for monetary policy.

Since the July meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), by far the greatest driver of higher yields has been an increase in term premium – the extra compensation investors demand to hold longer-dated government debt amid elevated uncertainty. Second to that, it’s robust economic activity. Notably, and in contrast to most media narratives, upward pressure from explicitly more hawkish monetary policy hasn’t been a factor. The U.S. 30-year Treasury yield has risen over 20 basis points since the July FOMC meeting. At the same time, Brent crude has risen approximately 13% in response to developments in the Middle East. On the surface, rangebound oil prices six months into the conflict in Iran haven’t spooked markets in the same way they did in March. Even with escalation in the Middle East conflict, Brent crude has traded within a range of $80 to $100 per barrel, to which both financial markets and the economy have adapted. Instead, the pressure is building underneath the hood – in the refined products space. Whereas oil and gasoline prices have risen 32% and 37%, respectively, since the conflict began, diesel and jet fuel have risen by much more – by 50% and 60%, respectively. The problem is that the United States, although oil-rich and currently the largest producer and exporter of oil in the world, primarily has light crude. American refineries, largely built to convert heavy crude into those refined products, are nearing their maximum capacity. So even though light crude is readily available, it doesn’t necessarily alleviate the rising prices of those refined products, or the potential readthrough into more consumer-facing products like airfares. The relationship has created a synergy between refining margins and bond yields. As investors measure the impact of the conflict, the building relationship shows pressure in that part of the commodities market is starting to align with the move in bond yields. Higher energy prices across products are not necessarily signaling an imminent downturn. Instead, they’re reinforcing a market environment where growth remains firm enough to support consumer resilience and spending. That’s partially why term premiums have continued to rise. For equity investors, the key risk is not necessarily higher oil prices but higher discount rates that materialize quickly rather than gradually – especially as autumn approaches and the stock market faces what has historically been stocks’ weakest month of the year. Seasonality is often dismissed as market folklore, but many calendar effects are rooted in predictable flows. Tax deadlines, pension contributions, portfolio rebalancing, corporate buybacks and options expiries all occur on known schedules, creating recurring shifts in liquidity and investor positioning. These dynamics rarely drive markets on their own, but they can amplify existing trends – like the effect of a move in bond yields – and tend to set the final quarter of the year up for gains. The recent rise in bond yields is a reminder that not all inflation risks originate with monetary policy. Growing pressure in refined products markets, alongside resilient economic activity and higher term premiums, suggests the bond market and its effects across other financial spheres are responding to a broader set of forces than simply the path of Fed rate cuts. As large-cap sponsors scale multi-strategy credit platforms, they are changing how liquidity is created, distributed and tested under stress. Financial sponsors have fundamentally transformed their role in global credit markets, evolving from classic buyout specialists into multi-strategy asset managers. New models build on classic buyout funds to include direct lending funds, credit vehicles, secondaries and more. As a result, sponsors are increasingly both users and providers of credit, influencing both sides of the credit transaction. This expansion into credit strategies is motivated by shifting capital structures. Most companies have more debt than equity, driving down limited partner (LP) demand and drawing sponsors toward credit strategies. These include: This isn’t a zero-sum reallocation. “The market’s evolving. But all three of those sleeves — loans, high-yield bonds and private credit — have grown dramatically over the last 25 years,” said Jake Pollack, head of North America Credit Trading and Global Credit Financing at J.P. Morgan. “We expect them to continue to grow over the next 10 years.” “Loans, high-yield bonds and private credit have grown dramatically over the last 25 years. We expect them to continue to grow over the next 10 years.” Head of North America Credit Trading and Global Credit Financing, J.P. Morgan The most consequential structural development is the emergence of two distinct but increasingly interconnected credit regimes operating within the same market: public and private credit. “To some extent, when the broadly syndicated market was more challenged, it could feel like public and private markets were an either-or choice. That’s not the case not anymore,” said Pollack. “Borrowers have options to look at both markets. That's going to continue to be a theme as we go forward." Sponsors and their portfolio companies increasingly maintain a presence in both markets, deploying capital where conditions are most favorable. This dual approach allows for greater agility and resilience, especially as market cycles shift. Syndicated loan and high-yield bond markets offer price discovery, but access is conditional on market windows remaining open. Direct lending, by contrast, operates through compressed decisioning — a smaller group of counterparties negotiating terms directly with the borrower, reducing execution risk and timeline uncertainty. The trade-off is cost: private credit typically prices at a premium to public market alternatives when conditions are favorable. The governance dimension is where the two regimes diverge most sharply in structural terms. Public market instruments are governed by standardized documentation and distributed investor consent thresholds. Private credit operates under negotiated governance: lenders and borrowers agree to bespoke covenants, amortization schedules, call protection and reporting requirements at origination. This creates tighter alignment between lender and borrower in stable conditions, but concentrates amendment and restructuring authority in a smaller group when conditions deteriorate. Broadly syndicated loans and high-yield bonds benefit from continuous, observable pricing through secondary market activity. Private credit assets, by contrast, are marked infrequently and often at model-derived valuations. This creates an information asymmetry that can complicate real-time assessment of portfolio quality and market-clearing levels during periods of dislocation. This is where regime differences carry the most significant market-structure implications. “Public markets may reprice or effectively shut for new deals, while private credit can sometimes continue lending because it relies less on daily market demand and more on negotiated relationships,” said Pollack. Concentrated ownership, infrequent trading and fewer observable prices mean that stress in private credit portfolios tends to surface through amendments, covenant waivers and restructurings rather than through secondary market repricing — a dynamic that can obscure the true state of credit quality until adjustment is unavoidable. The expansion of sponsor-led credit strategies has been accompanied by a parallel scaling of the infrastructure used to distribute and finance those assets. Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) have become the dominant vehicle for broadly syndicated leveraged loans, with the Financial Stability Board reporting that the U.S. CLO market totaled $977 billion as of October 2026. This represents a significant share of outstanding issuance and shapes pricing, refinancing timelines and covenant norms across the market. Securitization techniques are now being applied to private credit at scale. Business development companies (BDCs), interval funds and private credit CLOs (PCLOs) are packaging direct lending assets into rated, tranched structures. This is in turn broadening the investor base, freeing up capital for new origination and deepening the structural integration of private credit into rated capital markets. The structural divergence between public and private credit regimes has direct consequences for capital structure design, refinancing risk and how investors assess credit quality. The availability of both public and private credit channels creates genuine optionality in capital structure design. Borrowers who have accessed private credit for execution certainty have increasingly needed to weigh governance terms against operating flexibility. Maturity profile management has emerged as a distinct risk dimension given the refinancing dynamics of each regime. Sponsors increasingly operate across both public and private channels simultaneously, with portfolio companies borrowing via syndicated markets, direct lending facilities and securitized vehicles at the same time. For borrowers operating across both channels, maintaining independent public market access functions as a structural hedge, one that preserves optionality when private credit conditions or counterparty relationships shift. Perhaps the most important implication is the need for regime awareness: a clear-eyed understanding of which credit channel is being accessed, under what governance terms, with what liquidity characteristics and through what stress pathway. As default rates remain relatively low, the structural differences between regimes can appear immaterial. However, history suggests they become more consequential when conditions change, testing underwriting standards, deal structures and investor assumptions about liquidity simultaneously. The next phase of sponsor-led credit market growth will be shaped by how well all participants — sponsors, borrowers, investors and intermediaries — navigate the interaction between these two regimes. “The priority is not to choose between them, but to understand the structural logic of each and plan accordingly,” said Pollack. Alan Bunting left developer this spring after decade at business British Land’s former head of development delivery Alan Bunting has become the next major name to land a key role on JP Morgan Chase’s plan to build a new headquarters building in Canary Wharf. Bunting left British Land in the spring but Building understands he has now joined the banking giant in a managing director role working on its new HQ. JP Morgan Chase declined to comment. Bunting joined British Land a decade ago as a project director from Ramboll and was promoted to head of development delivery nearly seven years ago before leaving at the end of March. Alan Bunting has been appointed to a managing director role on JP Morgan Chase’s plan for a new HQ in Canary Wharf In the summer, Alinea co-founder Steve Watts, who was also a long-standing chair of the Council on Tall Buildings, joined JP Morgan as its cost and commercial managing director for the building at Riverside South. JP Morgan has been putting together a team to build the tower designed by Foster & Partners with Watts being the first high-profile recruit. No details of how tall the tower will be or what it will look like have been released but it is understood Fosters had originally come up with three options and what is known is that it will run across three million sq ft and be home to 12,000 employees while flight path regulations in the area mean it cannot be more than 265m high. Earlier this year, Building revealed that Gardiner & Theobald had been appointed to a cost consultancy role on the scheme. The firm has been helping out with early feasibility work although that is understood to have now finished. The cost of the JP Morgan scheme has been put at £10bn and will be built on the Riverside South plot that was due to be developed by the bank nearly 20 years ago before being put on hold because of the financial crash. JP Morgan then moved into a building on the estate previously occupied by failed Wall Street bank Lehman Brothers, paying £495m for the site in 2010. It also leases space at 1 Cabot Square. But, according to insiders, the bank, which also has a site at Victoria Embankment near Blackfriars, is “bursting at the seams” at its 25 Bank Street site and settled on Riverside South after looking at locations in both the City and Canary Wharf. London tower builders have put the plans on their radar with JP Morgan understood to be mulling whether to use contractors like Mace and Multiplex for the job – or stick to Canary Wharf Contractors which has carried out much of the building work at the Docklands estate over the years. title: Internship Spotlight: Kate Lowenstein ’27, J.P. Morgan - Yale School of Management
content:
Core courses and support from the Finance Club helped Kate Lowenstein ’27 pivot into finance with a summer internship at an investment bank. Internship: J.P. Morgan, New York CityHometown: Duluth, GeorgiaPronouns: she/her/hersSOM class I used on the job: Sourcing & Managing FundsGo-to work lunch: SweetgreenAfter-work routine: Attempting to unwind, then getting to bed so I could do it all again the next morning!Favorite thing about my internship city: A summer in New York with so many SOM friends nearby. Two years ago, I was teaching algebra in a New York City public high school. This summer, I hit the desk at J.P. Morgan, working on live deals in the consumer and retail group. It was a pretty big change, to say the least. Before business school, I spent two years with Teach For America and briefly worked in consulting. I came to SOM interested in pivoting into finance, and investment banking was a completely new world to me. When recruiting started last fall, even the vocabulary felt new. J.P. Morgan quickly became one of the places I was most excited about. I was drawn to the scale of the firm and the opportunity to work across some of the most interesting transactions in the market. Before starting, though, I was nervous. After surviving teaching algebra to over 150 ninth-graders, I knew I could work hard. But I had never worked at an investment bank. I wondered whether I would know enough on day one or be able to keep up with peers who had a finance background. That is where SOM made such a difference. Classes like Sourcing & Managing Funds and Basics of Accounting gave me a strong foundation and helped me feel much more confident walking into the technical parts of the job. Just as important was the Finance Club. Second-year students and mentors helped prepare us for all the things that are harder to learn in a classroom: how to navigate a new team, ask good questions, manage competing priorities, and understand what being a great associate actually looks like. Over my nine weeks on the job, I got exposure to projects across M&A, equity, and debt, and I was constantly learning. The Consumer & Retail group advises many of the brands people interact with every day, across industries like retail, restaurants, food and beverage, and consumer products. We help these companies navigate transactions and other strategic decisions. I loved the pace of the group. There was always something happening, and I got to work alongside people who knew these companies and industries incredibly well. I saw the Yale network show up throughout my summer. I was lucky enough to work in the same group as Drew Walker, an SOM alum and former Finance Club president, who became a great resource and mentor. I also had the opportunity to work on a deal with Jonathan Dunlop, another SOM alum and a senior banker at the firm. It was pretty amazing to go from relying on SOM second-years during recruiting to suddenly working alongside Yale alumni on actual deals. People warned me before the summer about the hours in banking—and yes, there are long days. What surprised me was how much I enjoyed the work. When you are working on an interesting deal with a team you like, there is an energy to it that is hard to replicate. Somewhere along the way, the career pivot I had been working toward since arriving at SOM stopped feeling like a pivot and started feeling like my actual career. I came into the summer hoping I would like investment banking. I left knowing I wanted to come back. I was fortunate to receive and accept a return offer, and after graduation I’ll be heading back to J.P. Morgan in New York. It is exciting to think that something that felt completely unfamiliar when I arrived at SOM last fall is now the beginning of my next chapter. For anyone coming to SOM hoping to make a big career change: It can feel intimidating at first. Ask the questions, lean on your classmates and second-years, and don’t assume that everyone else knows more than you do. SOM gave me the technical foundation, the mentors, and—most importantly—the confidence to make a transition I wasn’t sure was possible. And keep a coffee order ready—you’ll need that too! title: Toto, I don’t think it’s the Fed anymore - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The upward march in bond yields continues to drive the market narrative. But the logic has shifted. The initial move began in the early summer with a Federal Reserve that investors initially perceived as hawkish, but a series of softer jobs and inflation reports has cast a different spotlight. Now, the drivers look a little different. It’s a combination of worries around global fiscal deficits, an increase in hyperscaler issuance and the rise of refined product prices. That’s on top of economic growth in the U.S. economy. Using a sign-restriction model that determines the drivers of Treasury yields on any given day based on how yields behave relative to inflation expectations, the dollar and equity markets, different combinations can help distinguish whether higher yields reflect stronger growth, rising term premiums or changing expectations for monetary policy. Different combinations can help distinguish whether higher yields reflect stronger growth, rising term premiums or changing expectations for monetary policy. Since the July Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, by far the greatest driver of higher yields has been an increase in term premium: the extra compensation investors demand to hold longer-dated government debt amidst elevated uncertainty. Second to that, it’s robust economic activity. Notably, and in contrast to most media narratives, upward pressure from explicitly more hawkish monetary policy hasn’t been a factor. Sources: JPM WM Solutions. Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of September 2, 2026. 
Note: Data based on a sign-restriction model. Model determines driver on any given day based on how the 10-year yield moves relative to inflation expectations, the USD and the S&P 500. The U.S. 30-year yield has risen over 20 basis points since the July FOMC meeting. At the same time, Brent crude has risen approximately 13% in response to developments in the conflict in the Middle East.

On the surface, rangebound oil prices six months into the conflict in Iran haven’t spooked markets the same way they did in March. Even with escalating conflict in the Middle East, Brent crude has traded within a range of $80 to $100, which both financial markets and the economy have adapted to. Instead, the pressure is building underneath the hood—in the refined products space.

Whereas oil and gasoline prices have risen 32% and 37%, respectively, since the conflict began, diesel and jet fuel have risen by much more, at 50% and 60%, respectively. The problem is that the United States, although oil-rich and currently the largest producer and exporter of oil in the world, primarily has light crude.

American refineries, largely built to convert heavy crude into those refined products, are nearing their maximum capacity. So, even though light crude is readily available, it doesn’t necessarily alleviate the rising prices of those refined products, or the potential readthrough into more consumer-facing products, like airfares.

The relationship has created a synergy between refining margins and bond yields. As investors measure the impact of the conflict, the building relationship shows pressure in that part of the commodities market is starting to align with the move in bond yields. Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of September 2, 2026.
Note: Average cost considers gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices. Higher energy prices across products are not necessarily signaling an imminent downturn. Instead, they’re reinforcing a market environment where growth remains firm enough to support consumer resilience and spending. That’s partially why term premiums have continued to rise. For equity investors, the key risk is not necessarily higher oil prices, but rather higher discount rates that materialize quickly, not gradually—especially as the autumn approaches, and the stock market faces what has historically been stocks’ weakest month of the year. Seasonality is often dismissed as market folklore, but many calendar effects are rooted in predictable flows. Tax deadlines, pension contributions, portfolio rebalancing, corporate buybacks and options expiries all occur on known schedules, creating recurring shifts in liquidity and investor positioning. These dynamics rarely drive markets on their own, but they can amplify existing trends—like the effect of a move in bond yields—but also tend to set the final quarter of the year up for gains. The recent rise in bond yields is a reminder that not all inflation risks originate with monetary policy. Growing pressure in refined products markets, alongside resilient economic activity and higher term premiums, suggests the bond market and its effect across other financial spheres is responding to a broader set of forces than simply the path of Fed rate cuts.
